title: Inter-Individual Variability in the Adaptive Responses to Endurance and Sprint Interval Training: A Randomized Crossover Study
authors: Bonafiglia JT, Rotundo MP, Whittall JP, Scribbans TD, Graham RB, Gurd BJ
population: Recreationally active adults completing both endurance (END) and sprint interval training (SIT) in randomized crossover with 3-month washout
findings: 21 recreationally active adults completed 3 weeks (4 days/week) each of END (30 min at ~65% VO2peak work rate) and SIT (eight 20-s intervals at ~170% VO2peak work rate).
A main effect of training was seen for VO2peak, lactate threshold and submaximal HR, but individual responses to both END and SIT were highly variable.

No significant positive relationships were observed between individual END and SIT changes in any variable; non-response (defined as change below 2x typical error: VO2peak 0.107 L/min, lactate threshold 15.7 W, submaximal HR 10.7 bpm) occurred after both, but the individual patterns differed.
All individuals responded in at least one variable under at least one of the stimuli; authors suggest non-response may be reduced by changing the training stimulus.
limitations: Small sample, 3-week interventions, cycling-based, healthy recreationally active adults (not runners); non-response defined by typical-error threshold on single measures.
implications: Responder status is not a stable trait across stimulus types: after a block with no measurable improvement, vary the stimulus before concluding that the athlete is a non-responder.
Judge response with a pre-specified measurement-noise threshold (e.g. 2x typical error of the measure) and several markers rather than a single metric.
